title: Notifications and Reporting
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of notifications and reporting and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to notifications and reporting.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on notifications and reporting. Workflow summaries and notifications should report outcome, useful run links, and sanitized context without creating duplicates or leaking secrets. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Notifications and Reporting matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Workflow summaries and notifications should report outcome, useful run links, and sanitized context without creating duplicates or leaking secrets. External integrations need explicit authentication, narrow permissions, input validation, rate-limit handling, deduplication, and safe reporting that does not leak credentials or payloads.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Workflow summaries and notifications should report outcome, useful run links, and sanitized context without creating duplicates or leaking secrets. External integrations need explicit authentication, narrow permissions, input validation, rate-limit handling, deduplication, and safe reporting that does not leak credentials or payloads. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Workflow summaries
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Pull request comments
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Issue creation
items.text: For issue creation, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Chat and messaging integrations
items.text: Use a scoped token, validate request inputs and event payloads, check HTTP/error status, handle pagination and rate limits, and avoid logging credentials or unneeded private response data.

items.title: Success and failure notifications
items.text: Use a scoped token, validate request inputs and event payloads, check HTTP/error status, handle pagination and rate limits, and avoid logging credentials or unneeded private response data.

content_blocks.code:
- name: Write a concise workflow summary
  run: |
    {
      echo "## Validation result"
      echo "- Status: passed"
      echo "- Commit: $GITHUB_SHA"
    } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
content_blocks.expected_output: The job summary shows a short validation heading, a status line, and the source commit.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use sanitized facts only. Write generated data through `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` and avoid dumping event payloads or environment variables.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet and remove temporary workflow changes. If you triggered a real run, inspect the run log before editing the file again.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to notifications and reporting. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain notifications and reporting, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Use GitHub APIs and CLI integration with explicit authentication, bounded permissions, and handled failures.

content.task: Apply notifications and reporting to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Workflow summaries and notifications should report outcome, useful run links, and sanitized context without creating duplicates or leaking secrets.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Workflow summaries and notifications should report outcome, useful run links, and sanitized context without creating duplicates or leaking secrets. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Workflow summaries and notifications should report outcome, useful run links, and sanitized context without creating duplicates or leaking secrets.
External integrations need explicit authentication, narrow permissions, input validation, rate-limit handling, deduplication, and safe reporting that does not leak credentials or payloads.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
